newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan Power vows to ship nuclear waste to N.Korea.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan Power vows to ship nuclear waste to N.Korea.

text.p: Taiwan's state power utility on Saturday said it would press ahead with plans to ship up to 200,000 barrels of nuclear waste to North Korea, ignoring a government council warning on possible diplomatic consequences.

"Our plan with North Korea would be carried out according to the contract, and Pyongyang has begun to send in details of the shipment's transport plans," a Taiwan Power Company (Taipower) executive told Reuters by telephone.
"At the moment, I don't see any change in our plan," he added.

His comment came after media reports on Friday that the Atomic Energy Council, which supervises Taipower's nuclear power plant operations, warned of possible diplomatic consequences if the deal went through.

Hu Ching-piao, chairman of the government's council, had considered abandoning the project because it may prove too costly to Taiwan's image and foreign relations, the state-funded Central News Agency reported.
Taipower's deal with Pyongyang to ship up to 200,000 barrels of low-radiation waste to Stalinist North Korea at a reported cost of US$230 million was signed in January 1997.
The Taipower official said that except for South Korea no other countries had loudly opposed the shipment plan.

South Korea, bitter rival of the North since the Korean War, has strongly opposed the plan, citing possible health hazards and fears of inadequate safety provisions in the communist North despite Taipower's assurance the nuclear waste was low in radiation.
It has sought international support, including that of the United States, to stop Taipower's plan. U.S. acting assistant secretary of state Charles Kartman has also expressed concern over the deal.

International environmental group Greenpeace has thrown its support behind South Korea, saying a recent secret inspection of the nuclear dump on Taiwan's Lanyu island showed the waste was not low in radiation as Taipower has claimed.
Most of Taiwan's nuclear waste is stored at the Lanyu dump.
Taipower denied the charges, saying it would not have signed the deal to ship the waste if it was not perfectly safe.
